value: the prevalence of depression symptoms in US adults during the first fortnight of the COVID-19 pandemic, set against a pre-pandemic national baseline measured with THE SAME INSTRUMENT
how much higher depression symptom prevalence was during COVID-19 than before it, and which social and economic resources predicted it
the first nationally representative before-and-during comparison of US depression symptoms on a single validated screener, and a severity gradient showing the increase is largest at the severe end

two probability-based population surveys compared cross-sectionally - NHANES 2017-2018 by household interview, and the CLIMB study of the AmeriSpeak online panel from 31 March to 13 April 2020 - both scored with PHQ-9, weighted, then multivariable logistic regression within the during-COVID arm
quote: This nationally representative survey study used 2 population-based surveys of US adults aged 18 or older. During COVID-19, estimates were derived from the COVID-19 and Life Stressors Impact on Mental Health and Well-being study, conducted from March 31, 2020, to April 13, 2020. Before COVID-19 estimates were derived from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, conducted from 2017 to 2018.
This survey study found that prevalence of depression symptoms in the US increased more than 3-fold during the COVID-19 pandemic, from 8.5% before COVID-19 to 27.8% during COVID-19.

This survey study found that prevalence of depression symptoms in the US increased more than 3-fold during the COVID-19 pandemic, from 8.5% before COVID-19 to 27.8% during COVID-19.

Our estimates of pre–COVID-19 depressive symptoms are consistent with other population-level nationally representative studies that captured different constructs of depression; in 2018, 4.7% of adults aged 18 years or older surveyed in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health had major depressive disorder with severe impairment, compared with 8.5% of adults in the NHANES having depression symptoms.

We assessed 13 stressors based on prior studies conducted after traumatic events. 20 , 21 Examples of COVID-19 stressors included losing a job, death of someone close to you owing to COVID-19, and having financial problems. We excluded stressors that were capturing constructs applicable only to specific groups and created a score ranging from 0 to 13 to measure cumulative exposure to COVID-19 stressors. We divided the scores into thirds to measure low, medium, and high exposure to COVID-19-induced stressors. Cutoffs for stressor score categories were low (score, 0-2), medium (score, 3-4), and high (score, 5-13).
